segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is your name in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Russell Beaver is my name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Dv-ni-no-li da-qua-do-i.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They call it Caney, Welling Road, that’s where I grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that’s where you grew up?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it a big town?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: We have five acres there. When I was one year old, we lived there. It was Grandpa’s land.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you have five acres?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you’ve been living there a long time?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: We moved when I was 16. We moved from there to Cookson, and lived there for 21 years. From there, I went to rehab back in June. When I came out of there, I went to live in Tahlequah. That’s where I live now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is that where you live now?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where have you worked?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I’ve worked a lot of different places. I always worked at Greenleaf off and on. When I get fired, then I start back a month later. [laughing] I lived in Tulsa, too, for about three years. I worked everywhere there too, what they call day labor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many are in your family?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Four girls, and three boys. My grandson still lives with me. He’s going to school at Sequoyah. I had two boys, but lost one to COVID about three years ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That was a mean one.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It took a lot of people.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: It took four days, then he passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was he in the hospital?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How old was he?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: He was 41 years old. My brother, a week later, he passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was his name?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Alex Junior.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was your daddy’s name?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Alex Beaver, Alegi they called him in Cherokee, and my mother, Irene Bunch was her name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they live toward the south?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Bunch, is Bunch toward the north?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess that’s what you would say.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Grandpa Arneecher, did you know him?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was his name?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: His name was Arneecher Beaver.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t think so.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Arneecher Beaver. I think he was from Watonga.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I think they live around Jay.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s where I’m from. People lived around there with that same name. They just died out. They just got old, that’s what happened.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And your parents live in Bunch?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s still a small town up there?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, uh-huh. There are still my first cousins there, named Pettit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The Pettits?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You know Dale Pettit?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Dale?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, I think that’s his name. He’s from Marble City. He goes to church there.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, sounds like I heard that name. I heard it before.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I went over there one time. They were having a meeting of different Cherokees, and others were there. What about your grandpa and grandmother? Are they still living?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, they are all gone. There was one named Narci, my daddy’s mother, who was my grandma, Narci Scraper. They are all from there, Bunch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were they farmers?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah, they talked about it. What do you call it? Cotton, or whatever it was, they used to pick that, I think, in the summertime.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about beans and strawberries, did they pick them?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I never heard them talk about beans, and Daddy and his father, my grandfather, made railroad ties for the better.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were talked about in Stilwell as growers.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I picked strawberries, but not that much.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Back then, there were a lot of Cherokees doing that, to help them financially. Your grandma, did she come from somewhere, or was she from around here?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: As far as I know, she was from around Bunch or Greasy. That’s where she lived and they grew up. Now, my mother’s dad, I didn’t know them that well, my grandpa.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Humm!

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Even their mother, I didn’t know. I was just little when they passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh… Can you tell me a little about yourself? When you were growing up and what you saw?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: My dad and I used to hunt a lot when we lived in Kansas [Oklahoma?], and we went fishing too, and we ran around together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about things in the woods? Did you hunt for food like squirrels?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Squirrel, yes, even deer. In the fall, we would find mushrooms.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wish!

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Dawoli.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Good to eat!

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Wild onions, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Onions, yeah! Onions that grow in the woods, did you sell them sometimes?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Shoot no! [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A lot of people do that, sell onions, and fish, too.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: There was somebody who came by and sold homemade cream.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ooh, mannn! Ooh, mannn!

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They were selling that. Mommy bought it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was really good! It’s hard to find some now. You can find it now, but it’s just like water. Just like you said, it was kind of hard.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: The bread was hard too! [laughing] We liked to go hunting, too. We had dogs that were good hunters. Even at night, we went hunting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where you lived, was it by the water?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, Caney Creek.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Caney Creek, was it a big creek all the time?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: All the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It never dried up?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Huh-uh, no.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess you went swimming there?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, yeah, we used to swim there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did your friends come over to go swimming?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes, we met there at the water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There were a lot of people at Caney Creek. I guess there were crawdads there?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, there were crawdads there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were good to eat.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah. They will chase you off now if you hunt crawdads. Or they will arrest you. [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I come from, you can only catch 12.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, 12, but not…

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: That’s just not enough.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nah! I guess you all could catch all you wanted.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you hunt them at night?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, we went fishing at night when Daddy was with us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is your dad still alive?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, they all passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They all passed away, even your mom?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah. I got one aunt, Daddy’s sister, that’s all I got.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you know anything about your dad when he was alive that you can talk about?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, just his work, and on weekends we’d go hunting. He drank a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My dad was the same way. He died from that, my dad.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: My dad quit when he turned 60, on his birthday. He said, “I’m going to quit.” I guess that’s when he quit. My dad smoked two packs a day. He said he was going to quit, and he never picked up a cigarette again, and he lived to be 80.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He just gave up then?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: What you call ‘Will Power’, he had that. You can do anything you want when you put your mind to it, he said to me. When I was in rehab, that’s what Sasa told me, “When you decide to do it, you can do it.” That’s what he said. When you decide.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: What would you call ‘Will Power’? What would you call it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess, if you’re willing to quit, if you have the strength in you. But you have to decide for yourself if that’s what’s in your heart, if you strive for it. It starts from the heart if it’s strong will…

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: If you really want it, you can do it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you decide.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes, if you decide.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you don’t give up. A lot of them, it’s hard for smokers to quit. It will take time.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: It’s been a month since I quit. I wasn’t strong enough. I prayed for strength to quit. Yeah, it’s been a month since I quit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I also went to rehab, June of last year. Seven months clean today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it because of your smoking?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: The other. [laughing] I was drinking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oooh! Did it handicap you?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, just about anything. I didn’t have nothing to show for it today. But I’m gaining it back, though.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Good, you’re doing well. Don’t give up.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: My wife and I together, we both went into rehab. I went first, then the boy came back well. We’re all doing well.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Good! Good, don’t give up, keep striving.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: We go to church at D. J., D. J. McCarter.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, in town. You’re doing good. What is your name again in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Dv-ni-no-li.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dv-ni-no-li, yeah. What was the reason they gave you that name?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Daddy gave us all our Cherokee names. Why he did, I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t know what the meanings are?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, and why he gave me that name, I don’t know, because I’m nasty, I guess. [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your wife, what is her Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Who?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your wife.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: She told me, but I forgot. Her last name is Snell, her maiden name. Woody Snell is her dad. Did you know him?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: That was his name, Woody Snell. He passed before I got to know him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I don’t know if that’s a good thing. [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was he a drinker too?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If someone asks you what your wife’s name was, are they talking about your wife’s - cook’s - name? That’s what they would say a long time ago.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, I’ve heard that before. Now, when they were going to start drinking, they used to call it “Put your tongue to it.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Put your tongue to it?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember long ago they would say, “Let’s drink again.”

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They would say, “Let’s drink again.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did your friends do that too?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Oh yeah, that’s all we knew what to do.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Your friends you grew up with, how are they now?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Just about all my drinking buddies have quit drinking now. And a lot of them have passed on.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess the rest of them are okay.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You seeing them, did that do something to your heart to quit?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Man, I don’t know about that, but you just spent a lot of money on that. I used to go to the casino. I wish I hadn’t done that, because I thought I might lose my wife doing that. There was nothing going right for us. But now that we quit, we’re doing better.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you were to talk to someone who drinks, what would you say to them?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I would just tell them it’s not any good. I would tell them what I did and what happened to me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Would you tell them all of what would happen? What would you tell them?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I would tell him, “Leave it alone,” and try to take him to church. That’s all I could do. It would be up to him to make that decision. You can tell a person anything about wanting them to quit drinking, but it’s up to him if he wants to quit. He’s got to want it himself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did someone talk to you?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No. I just did it on my own. I didn’t tell anybody, I just left, I didn’t even tell my wife I was going. I was in there for a while before she found out, my wife.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your past as you were growing up? Things you saw in your past as you were growing up, do you have something to tell them? Like if you have grandchildren, “This is my past and you should be aware,” or [are you] careful of things to tell people?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I already told them what happened as I grew up. And some I did that wasn’t good. They told me just about everything as I was growing up. They disciplined me as I was growing up. They always got after me for drinking around, but I didn’t listen. Until I saw myself doing what I was doing. I was hardheaded.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did your daddy ever tell you about the land that was allotted long time ago when it began? Some of them got over 300 acres.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, I never heard about that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You know this was long ago. Your grandparents or their parents would know, they gave out land back then.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, I didn’t know anything about helping out, that Cherokee Nation giving out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, this is not Cherokee Nation, this was the government. This is what they did a long time ago. Just like Eastern Cherokee, when we left and came out here.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I was never told that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, no one ever told you about how Eastern Cherokee left?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: A little bit. Daddy mentioned it here and there about the Trail of Tears.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He didn’t tell you anything about where it started? About when we left Eastern Cherokee?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I really don’t know what happened there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That land that you have, I mean your dad, your parents had, did they just buy it themselves?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I think so. Now Eagle, Sammy Eagle, if I go get the papers, the deed papers, if I bring them to him, he said that’s land no one can take away from me, he said. No one can live there but me. I thought we were going to lose it, if nobody moved on that land. I plan on moving there, but I’m having trouble buying a trailer house. Sammy said he was going to help me. But there are a lot of family members that own the land. There’s five acres, but there’s too many of us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: There’s too many heirs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s restricted land?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, would they…

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Will they dig a well, will Cherokee Nation help you? Or do you have to have a deed in your name before they can help you, Mom said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I really don’t know, I don’t know how that works. If you would check on it, that’s what they would tell you. That would be good, but they all would have to agree on it.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. That’s the way with me. It’s not much land.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: When one dies, there are more heirs. Their children and grandchildren.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is there deer on the land that you all own?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, but I haven’t hunted there in a while.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: We have killed many deer there. There’s probably bears there too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Uh-huh. There’s mean ones up there. What about wild hogs, do they live up there too?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, I don’t think they live there, but at Dry Creek I killed one, years back.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was he a big one?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, he wasn’t a big one, but he was a fat one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. They say they are mean and will chase you.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: [inaudible]…it used to be.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about when you were growing up? Starting when you were a little boy, were there a lot of people that lived by your house and other houses?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Not really, there were some, but they were old already.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: A couple. A-ni-ta was her name who lived there, she was an old woman. We lived behind her, and Terrapins lived nearby. There were two houses there, there were grown-ups living there, no children. We lived there by ourselves.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. I guess you all helped one another that were living close?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I guess so. Mom was friends with one of the women there. They used to can stuff.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Long time ago, people came together [in] Gadugi, and they all helped one another. When someone was sick or someone passed away, the neighbors came over.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They all helped one another.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is that what they did?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: That’s the way it was. We would go to help out, too. I really didn’t know what was going on, they just took me. When they got there, they helped the family there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some of them would stay two nights with them helping them out. I guess that’s the way it was?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah. I was too little back then to remember, but we would stay there two nights when someone passed away or was sick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. I guess if you remember back then, you would say there was not that much sickness when you were growing up.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Not really. There’s more today, isn’t there?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh, sickness. Back then, they just all walked, was it that way?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeeeah, not that much back then when I was growing up. He had a car, or we had a car. They really weren’t walking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess you had a place for a garden?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: No, we really didn’t have a garden.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh, some of them were gardeners, a long time ago.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: That Sinitsi, the old lady I talked about, used to plant a garden. My mom’s friend.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. What about when you were growing up? You said, where you used to live, can you remember something that was good that happened growing up, and then something bad in your life and you overcame it?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Bad things happening all the time. [laughing] Good times was when we ate chicken. [laughing] I don’t know, I mean - I don’t know. Seems like everyone was happy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I mean, we were poor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They didn’t have money, Mommy and Daddy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But you came through it?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. We made it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What I’m saying, or you were saying earlier, when they were canning, they would use mason jars, and they put them up as you said, what all did you can?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Apples, I think. Peaches. Mommy and the old lady helped one another when they were canning things. Even fish, they would can them too. Cucumbers, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Beans, too?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Beans too, green beans.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Potatoes, too?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Potatoes too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: On Thanksgiving, did they open them up?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I guess so, Thanksgiving and on Christmas.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what Mom used to do.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They used to can wild onions too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess they tasted good too, didn’t they?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Oh yeah, heck yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. They were good to eat, what you are talking about.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Oh yeah, and poke salad, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about watercress, did you all ever eat it?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, we used to love to eat it. They called it ‘fire in the water.’

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Was there spring water by your house?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, there was a spring there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. I guess you found watercress there?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Wild onions there, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you ever grow corn?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Mommy and Daddy didn’t make a garden, but the old lady [inaudible]. She would plant anything - corn, beans.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, back then, they would do that.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: [inaudible]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. How many of your children in your family speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: My children?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your children and your brothers?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: All my family, my brothers and my sisters, we all speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: And some of the girls. Their family speaks Cherokee too. My children don’t. Some of them understand Cherokee, but they don’t speak it. Now, my sister’s children speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where do they live?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Everywhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Everywhere?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah. Some live in Tahlequah, some in Stilwell, Dry Creek too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, some of them don’t go to school here? [Durbin Feeling Language Center]

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They used to. Some of them went to school here. My niece Wanda went to school here. There was one going over here at Sequoyah, Kentra, but she dropped out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Did you work here somewhere close?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Greenleaf. I was 16 years old when I started.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you started?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I was 16 when I started.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess they’re still around that you worked with at Greenleaf?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, some come to see me that I worked with.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. I know one of them who works there. His last name is Vann.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Vann? It isn’t, oh it isn’t, I might know who it is, what’s his name?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Farris.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Farris?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Farris Vann, he’s my cousin.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I’ll be!

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, I knew that’s who you were talking about when you said Vann. [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He’s been working there for a long time.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it about an hour?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: We still got a little time, about 40, 47 minutes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about what you see the Cherokee speaking? Do you think it’s going to grow more with them going to school here, in your opinion?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: In my opinion, no.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Why not?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: The White people. Where, I mean, where will they speak it, where will they be speaking it? I don’t think it’s going to grow, myself. [Cherokee language]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t think so?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: They are embarrassed to talk Cherokee, our people today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah. Do you think the ones who are going to school learning Cherokee, mixing it with English speaking - that English and Cherokee will work together?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If they use both of them, speaking in Cherokee and in English. Do you believe that’s going to happen?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: If they pass a law to speak Cherokee all the time, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: What about you, what do you think?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, it can, but they are going to have to work at it.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: I know a lot of older men living, many of them don’t even speak the language anymore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Indians…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Cherokee Indians.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. Well, where I grew up, all they spoke was Cherokee. Where I grew up at home, my mother and my brothers, we all spoke Cherokee.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: My daddy, when he was alive, he spoke Creek also. My grandfather was a full-blood Creek.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah. When I first started school, I didn’t speak English. As I continued school, I began speaking both Cherokee and English. I managed to finish school.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Well, you did good then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah. Like we were saying a while ago, if it’s coming from your heart, it’s going to happen, if you don’t give up. If everything is going good like you want it to, He is going to hear you [God]. Sometimes you have to go through hard times. As we were saying it will happen if it’s coming from the heart.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: It will happen, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And I’m thinking these ones that are going to school, I think they can do both Cherokee and English if they try. We are losing our Cherokee language.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There’s very few of us left. Huh-uh. Our elders…

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: We better hurry up, ain’t? Once we die…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. That’s why they are fighting to keep the school going, not to fail. To rise. That’s what I see.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah. That’s what I see.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. If we believe, it’ll happen, just like we said a while ago.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Uh-huh. If they don’t give up. If you pray, it will happen.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What we are saying, we are recording. One day, they are going to hear you speaking. They are going to hear something they can use and the way you spoke, and will study it in the future, something they can learn from. That is why I asked you all these questions. Somewhere, they are going to find or learn from you speaking. I think something is going to happen. My speaking, it’s going to help someone.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: It might help someone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. That’s right.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: When they find out. [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. What you were saying when you were growing up, striving to quit your addiction, someone will listen to that and help them out.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Something to help them as they listen to you speaking. It’ll be good.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes, in our speaking, they will find something to help them. I’ve seen a lot speaking to the elders when they were living, and speaking I found something that would help us.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, like today when my parents lectured me, I still use that…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Even though they are long gone…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: What they told me I use today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. They knew what they were talking about and there was a reason.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: This is the way it’s going to happen, I was told, and sure enough, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. I’m glad we talked, and glad we got to know one another.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Me too, I’m glad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Strive on. And speak Cherokee as much as possible, like to your children and your grandchildren. As much as you know, speak Cherokee. And they can learn to speak Cherokee if you do that.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Do you know Chris Holmes? Do you know Chris? He teaches Cherokee a little doesn’t he?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Uh-huh, here at Sequoyah.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: My grandchild that I told you is living with me, we are not related, but I am raising him. He’s 16 years old now. We are not related, but I’m raising him and he’s learning Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Is he speaking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Not very much, but Chris is teaching him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: He hasn’t learned that much yet, because he’s not Cherokee. [laughing]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, uh-huh.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Well, I’m glad we got to talk.

segments.speaker: russell-beaver
segments.translation: Is that it?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Good.
